analysis.one_liner: Requires health care companies to meet cybersecurity standards and pays hospitals to protect patient data.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final weeks of the 118th Congress, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every company handling health data — insurers, hospitals, and data clearinghouses — to meet federal minimum security standards, run annual stress tests, publish its security status, undergo independent audits, and pay fees and fines when it falls short. It would also give hospitals Medicare money to adopt cybersecurity practices and let Medicare send emergency advance payments to providers whose billing is knocked out by a hack. It was introduced with two Democratic senators and no Republican support, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never acted on before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients whose medical records and billing flow through a handful of large data systems. The bill would force the companies holding that data to meet minimum security requirements, publicly disclose their security status, and pass independent audits, and it would send money to hospitals — prioritizing rural, Puerto Rico, and other high-needs hospitals — to adopt security practices. Providers hit by a cyberattack could get Medicare advance payments to keep operating while claims processing is down.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients whose medical records are held digitally

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Health and Human Services Secretary to adopt minimum security requirements for all covered entities and business associates, and tougher requirements for companies whose failure would destabilize the health system, effective two years after enactment.

Requires each covered entity and business associate to run an annual security risk analysis, stress-test its ability to keep providing patient care after a cyber incident, file a CEO-signed compliance statement, and post its security status publicly in machine-readable form.

Requires annual independent security audits of every covered entity and authorizes the Secretary to audit at least 20 companies per year, focusing on systemically important firms and repeat violators.

Raises civil penalties for security-standard violations into higher fixed tiers and directs the Secretary to create a method for paying a share of collected penalties to individuals harmed by the violation.

Provides $800 million in Medicare payments for 2027-2028 and $500 million for 2029-2030 to help hospitals adopt essential and enhanced cybersecurity practices, targeting high-needs hospitals including rural, Puerto Rico, and Indian Health Service facilities.

Lets Medicare make accelerated and advance payments to hospitals, nursing homes, home health agencies, and other providers whose claims processing is significantly disrupted by a cybersecurity incident.
Funds the oversight program through user fees on covered entities, capped at $40 million in fiscal 2026 and $50 million in fiscal 2027, rising with inflation thereafter.

analysis.who_pays: Health care companies that hold or process patient data — insurers, hospital systems, pharmacies, and data clearinghouses — would pay user fees, compliance and audit costs, and larger fines, with civil penalties up to $5,000 per day for reporting failures and criminal penalties up to $1 million and 10 years for knowingly filing false security statements. Hospitals that do not adopt the required cybersecurity practices would face Medicare payment reductions of up to 1 percent. Some of these costs would likely be passed on through premiums and prices, and the incentive payments are drawn from the Medicare Hospital Insurance Trust Fund.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, hospitals, and health data clearinghouses

drawbacks.text: The bill bars any administrative or judicial review of how the Secretary decides which companies are systemically important, which payment methodology applies, and whether a hospital qualifies for a hardship exception — leaving those decisions unchecked by any reviewer.

Compliance, audit, and fee costs fall on every covered entity down to small practices, and while the Secretary may grant waivers where the burden outweighs the benefit, costs are likely to be passed to consumers through premiums and charges.
The $1.3 billion in hospital incentive payments are drawn from the Medicare Hospital Insurance Trust Fund, using Medicare dollars for cybersecurity upgrades rather than care.
The bill would create a permanent new annual audit industry around health data compliance, an ongoing cost the health sector would bear indefinitely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: health data breaches and ransomware attacks that freeze billing and interrupt care keep growing, and current HIPAA security rules are decades old with little enforcement. The bill pairs mandates with money — hospitals get help paying for upgrades rather than just penalties. The main honest objections are the unchecked bureaucratic discretion baked into the design and the likelihood that compliance costs flow to consumers. On balance, a serious attempt to fix a problem that has directly harmed patients.

outcome.mechanism: Wyden introduced the bill with Warner in late September 2024, near the end of the two-year Congress; the Senate Finance Committee never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on September 25, 2024, by Sen. Wyden, with Sen. Warner as the sole cosponsor.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the day it was introduced, and no further action was ever recorded.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without the committee holding a hearing or markup and without the bill ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that hold and process Americans' health records are better off: no new minimum security standards, annual audits, public disclosure of their security posture, user fees, or larger fines were ever imposed on them. Patients remain exposed to the same data-security landscape the bill was written to change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data-holding health companies, spared new security mandates

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon (D), bill's sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 25, 2024, and it was referred to the Finance Committee, which he chairs.

for.name: Mark Warner
for.role: U.S. Senator from Virginia (D), original cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsor joined; no vote ever occurred, so the partisan shape of the full Senate was never tested.

industries.industry: Health data clearinghouses and insurers (covered entities and business associates)
industries.note: These companies would face mandatory minimum security standards, annual independent audits, public disclosure of their security status, user fees, and larger fines. Their interest in avoiding those requirements runs against the public's interest in protecting medical records and keeping billing systems online, as large health-sector hacks have repeatedly disrupted patient care.

industries.industry: Hospitals, especially rural and high-needs hospitals
industries.note: Hospitals would receive up to $1.3 billion in Medicare incentive payments to adopt cybersecurity practices, with priority for rural, Puerto Rico, Indian Health Service, and other high-needs facilities, while facing modest Medicare payment cuts if they decline to adopt. The payments target exactly the hospitals least able to fund security upgrades on their own.

industries.industry: Independent healthcare cybersecurity audit and consulting firms
industries.note: The bill would require every covered entity and business associate to contract an independent auditor annually, creating a large, permanent compliance market. The audits are meant to surface weaknesses that endanger patient data, so the new revenue is tied to the public's protection.
